forces: Mixed chorus and orchestra with organ
performers: Wiener Staatsopernchor; Wiener Philharmoniker; Franz Sauer, organ; Bruno Walter, conductor
recorded: 26 July 1956, Small Festival Hall, Salzburg; live
intro: The Dies irae, marked Allegro assai, is the third section of the Requiem in D minor, K. 626, in which the choir sings the text of the Day of Judgement over rapid string figures. Bruno Walter conducts the Vienna forces in Süssmayr’s completion.

sections.label: A · Choir in four parts, Allegro assai
sections.mNote: Four choral parts enter together over fast strings.

sections.label: B · Repeated notes in the basses
sections.mNote: Repeated bass notes break into the upper voices’ phrases.

sections.label: C · All four voices together
sections.mNote: All four voices move to the close in D minor.

cues.title: Opening of the Dies irae
cues.text: The four choral parts enter together in D minor on “Dies irae”, day of wrath, the opening of the Latin Requiem Sequence. The violins play repeated notes and the bass moves in broken chords. Trumpets and timpani mark the beat.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1877), Dies irae, bars 1–8; Martin Norbäck’s public-domain engraving: https://www.mutopiaproject.org/ftp/MozartWA/KV626/dies_irae/dies_irae-a4.pdf. The text is the opening of the Latin Requiem Sequence.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: “Quantus tremor”, choral basses
cues.text: The choral basses sing “Quantus tremor” — how great the trembling — on repeated notes set against the beat, beginning in the second half of bar 40. Sopranos, altos and tenors reply with the words of the day of wrath. The violins keep up their fast figuration throughout.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1877), Dies irae, bars 40–49; Norbäck engraving, pp. 6–7. The basses begin their repeated-note figure in the second half of bar 40.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Instrumental close
cues.text: The choir stops after the first beat of bar 65, and bars 66–68 are for orchestra alone. Violins, bassoons and the bass line keep moving until the final D minor chord cuts them off.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1877), Dies irae, bars 65–68; Norbäck engraving, p. 9. The choir rests after the first beat of bar 65; bars 66–68 are wholly instrumental.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

transitions.title: Choir halts on A; basses lead on
transitions.from: A · Choir in four parts, Allegro assai
transitions.to: B · Repeated notes in the basses
transitions.how: The choir stops on A major, the dominant of D minor. The basses then sing a repeated figure alone, and the other three parts follow in longer notes. Bassoons double the bass line. The violins play quick repeated notes and then climb through the reply of the upper voices. The tempo remains Allegro assai.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1877), Dies irae, bars 40–49; Norbäck engraving, pp. 6–7.

transitions.title: Full choir at “Quantus tremor”
transitions.from: B · Repeated notes in the basses
transitions.how: All four choral parts take up “Quantus tremor”, with their repeated notes now sung together, and the orchestral bass resumes its running broken chords. Trumpets and timpani punctuate the return. The violins continue the fast pulse through the final judgement and the short D minor postlude.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel score (1877), Dies irae, bars 50–68; Norbäck engraving, pp. 7–9.

source.title: Mozart–Süssmayr, Dies irae, Martin Norbäck engraving after Breitkopf 1877
source.locator: Public-domain engraving, pp. 1–9: choral attacks over fast strings, the repeated-note bass passage at bars 40–49 and the orchestral close at bars 66–68.

timeline.note: The choir sings in block chords over fast string figures; trumpets and timpani play the accents.
Repeated choral bass notes alternate with longer replies from the upper voices; the violins keep moving.
All four choral parts take up Quantus tremor while the orchestral bass resumes its running broken chords.
After the last choral syllable, violins, bassoons and the bass line continue to the D-minor close.

fields.label: Performers
fields.value: Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor)
fields.note: This movement is for chorus, without a solo vocal part; the concert’s vocal solo quartet is not credited as singing here. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Traditional Mozart–Süssmayr completion, Dies irae; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified.
fields.note: Mozart left the vocal and bass framework and some instrumental indications; the traditional completed orchestration is used as the reference. The recording sources do not name a printed edition. The NMA preface quotes Walter’s policy of cutting some trombone doublings, but does not map it to this 1956 performance. The complete movement includes its orchestral postlude.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: The primary concert archive identifies Thursday 26 July 1956; Commons, Internet Archive and the discography agree. This is the live performance date, not the date of first publication, a later commercial issue, digitisation or upload.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Small Festival Hall (Kleines Festspielhaus), Salzburg, Austria
fields.note: The Vienna Philharmonic event archive supplies Small Festival Hall. Internet Archive calls the source a live Salzburg Festival performance; the discography uses the broader Festspielhaus designation. No studio session, microphone layout or original recording medium is inferred.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: The carrier actually used for this upload is unidentified. The discography lists Cetra, Nuova Era, Seven Seas and Orfeo issues of this performance. The official festival catalogue documents an Orfeo CD in 1996, but neither source ties that issue to the Ogg. A known issue is not a demonstrated transfer source.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: No catalogue number is attached to the transferred source. Cetra LO516, Nuova Era 2209, Seven Seas K30Y307 and Orfeo C430961B are documented release leads only. The festival catalogue dates Orfeo C 430 961 B to 1996; that is not evidence of first release or byte provenance.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: No matrix, take or side identifiers are supplied for the source used. The file is a complete movement from a live performance; neither a shellac carrier nor an original tape generation is established. No physical side join is assigned to a musical event.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: D. Benjamin Miller is the Commons uploader, not an established transfer or mastering engineer. The Internet Archive uploader/scanner fields document repository submission, not who digitised, edited or restored the recording. No transfer-engineer credit has been found.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: Internet Archive added/public date is 4 June 2018; Commons upload is 5 June 2018. These are not transfer dates. The embedded Commons digitising year 1956 duplicates the performance year without a transfer history and is not accepted as such evidence. The 1996 Orfeo issue is also not assigned as the date of this transfer.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Internet Archive lists the corresponding Ogg Vorbis movement file as an original upload; Commons supplies Ogg Vorbis and an MP3 access derivative.
fields.note: Here original means the repository’s uploaded file, not an original session master. The chain from the unidentified physical or broadcast source to the Ogg is undocumented. Session medium, tape generation, speed correction, equalisation, noise reduction, editing and restoration settings remain unknown; no such processing is inferred from the transfer’s sound.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0.
fields.note: The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to play the finale through. The work was K. 466 in D minor. It opens with syncopated strings, and the piano enters with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert excellent.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart later dedicated the quartets to him.
